p is the chance that the claim as written is right, as a model judged it. null means that no model has given one yet. It does not mean that the claim is in doubt. When any claim has a number, models.probabilities must name the model that gave it.

A reading file writes its claims and its passages the same way, so the two kinds of file read alike. A claim in a reading has one more backing mark, na, and more fields for what the claim says, such as against. A bounds claim takes neither.

docs.title: Passages
docs.text:
A quote is written once in the file, however many claims it backs. passages is keyed by number, a whole number of 1 or more. Each passage holds the quote and where it was read, in one of two ways.

Field Holds quote The words, copied from the source. It cannot be empty. record and field For a quote from a GEO record: the record, and the field of it. paper and section For a quote from a paper: the paper, and the section of it.

A passage has record and field, or it has paper and section. The check rejects a passage with only one of a pair, or with parts of both.

docs.title: Titles
docs.text:
titles maps each record that the file places to its title. A placed record is any record in series, in papers or in left_out, so a left-out record has its title too. Each title is copied from the record's GEO entry or from its paper, so that a reader of the file needs no record store.

  • A record with no title has no entry.
  • Each id under titles must be a record that the file places.
  • A title cannot be blank.

Titles are copied, not claimed. A title has no backing mark and no p.

docs.title: What the bounding job writes
docs.text:
The bounding job draws a study's bounds from its archive records and papers. Its files have this shape:

  • Code keeps the Series that the study starts from, or each sub-Series when the study starts from a SuperSeries. Code leaves each SuperSeries out. These claims are inferred, with a text that starts code:, and their p is null.
  • Jev is asked about every other linked Series and every linked paper, twice: once as the question is written, and once with the question reversed. A record is in the study when Jev answers yes to the question as written. Its claim is inferred. The text gives both of Jev's answers, and p is Jev's probability for the answer it gave.
  • passages is {}.
  • models names Jev for both roles when Jev was asked anything. When the linked records held nothing to ask about, both are null.
  • titles holds the title of each placed record, from its Series record or its paper.

A study ends unsettled when Jev's two answers about a record disagree. It ends refused when its linked records hold more than 50 Series, when Jev gives no answer about a record, or when the file fails the format check. Passes and the study workflow say how a run reports each ending.

docs.title: The 50 bounds files of the standard set
docs.text:
The 50 bounds.yaml files of the standard set were drawn before quotes and probabilities were part of the format, and they were converted to it. So in each of them:

  • every claim is inferred, and its text is the reason that the model wrote when it drew the study;
  • every p is null, and so is models.probabilities;
  • models.bounds names the model whose bounds became the study's;
  • passages is empty;
  • there are no titles, because the files were drawn before titles were copied.

The 50 job-bounds.yaml files beside them are the bounding job's own output, and each has titles.

docs.title: An example with every part
docs.text:
This example is made up to show every part of the format. Its quotes, numbers and model names are not real. It passes the check.

format: 1
study: GSE101112
models:
  bounds: example/model-a
  probabilities: example/model-b
series:
- id: GSE101112
  quoted: [1]
  p: 0.97
papers:
- pmid:31742554
left_out:
- id: pmid:33294943
  inferred: Software paper that uses the dataset only as test data
  see: [2]
  p: 0.9
- id: pmid:32884834
  unknown: Nothing that was read says whether it made new data
  p: null
reason: The 2019 paper made and reports the data held in this Series.
passages:
  1:
    paper: pmid:31742554
    section: Data availability
    quote: "RNA-seq data have been deposited in GEO under accession GSE101112"
  2:
    record: GSE101112
    field: Series_citation
    quote: "A tool paper that lists this Series among its examples"
titles:
  GSE101112: An example Series title
  pmid:31742554: An example paper title

docs.title: The check
docs.text:
seqforge study check-bounds <file> reads one file and prints one JSON object:

{
  "file": "bounds.yaml",
  "format": 1,
  "valid": false,
  "problems": [
    {"field": "series[0].quoted", "reason": "passage 7 does not exist"},
    {"field": "split_samples", "reason": "not a field of the format"}
  ]
}

file is the path you gave. format is the format number that the check accepts. Each problem names the field and the reason. series[0] is the first entry of series.

Exit code Meaning 0 The file is valid. 3 The file is rejected. problems lists why. 2 The file cannot be read. A file that is not UTF-8 text cannot be read.

The check also rejects these, each with exit code 3:

  • Text that is not YAML, or YAML that is not a mapping of fields. The problem's field is (file).
  • A wrong or missing format. The check asks about the format number first, and alone. A file with another number gets that one problem, which names the number that the check expected.
  • A key that one mapping writes twice. The problem names the key. Plain YAML keeps the last of the two and reports nothing, so a repeated field would go unseen.
  • A value of the wrong type. A value has the type that this page writes for it. The check rejects a number in quotes, such as p: "0.5", and true where a number belongs.

The check asks only whether the file is well formed. It does not open GEO, and it does not judge whether the bounds are right.

docs.title: When the format changes
docs.text:
There is one format at a time. format is a whole number, and the check accepts only the current one. A file with another number is rejected, and the message names the number that the check expected.

A change to the format raises the number and rewrites every existing file in the same change. No file stays behind in an older format. Git history is the only record of the old form.

titles came in without a new number. Every file without it stays valid, so no file had to be rewritten.

docs.title: The reading file
docs.text:
A study is one piece of research: the experiments that one paper reports, or one project that has no paper yet. The bounds file says which GEO Series and which papers belong to a study. GEO is the Gene Expression Omnibus, and a Series is one deposit of samples in it.

The study's reading says what each sequenced sample was: the species, the tissue, the treatment, the assay, and which labels the study varied between its samples. Each statement comes with the words that back it, the words that speak against it where the sources disagree, and a probability. The reading file writes the reading down, one file per study, in YAML, a plain-text format of fields and lists.

This page describes every field and every rule of the file. It is all you need to read one.

docs.title: A short example
docs.text:
This is part of the reading that the reading job wrote for the standard-set study GSE112068, a time course of human lung fibroblasts treated with the drug bleomycin. The job read only the GEO records. The excerpt keeps one factor, four shared claims and one of the 23 samples, and a comment marks each cut.

format: 2
study: GSE112068
models:
  reading: deepseek/deepseek-flash
  probabilities: typesafe/jev-1.14.0
read:
- records
read_detail: The records of GSE112068 and their 23 sequenced samples; no paper.
ontology_snapshot:
  source: 'liulab-data ontology store: cellosaurus-57.0, chebi-257, cl-2026-11-13, efo-3.96.0, hsapdv-2025-01-23,
    ncbitaxon-2026-11-26, pato-2026-10-01, uberon-2026-11-05'
  date: 2026-11-28
passages:
  # ... passages 1 to 3 cut
  4:
    record: GSE112068
    field: Series_summary
    quote: bleomycin at 0 ug/ml, 2 ug/ml and 40 ug/ml for 2 h
  5:
    record:
    - GSM3056966
    - GSM3056967
    - GSM3056968
    field: Sample_characteristics_ch1
    quote: 'dose: 0 ug/ml'
  # ... passages 6 to 20 cut
  21:
    record: each_sample
    field: Sample_library_strategy
    quote: RNA-Seq
  # ... passages 22 to 25 cut
  26:
    record: each_sample
    field: Sample_organism_ch1
    quote: Homo sapiens
factors:
  # ... the factors treatment and time_point cut
  dose:
    levels:
    - 0_ug_ml
    - 2_ug_ml
    - 40_ug_ml
    baseline: 0_ug_ml
    ordered: true
    quoted:
    - 4
    p: 0.99
shared:
  species:
    text: Homo sapiens
    term: NCBITaxon:9606
    quoted:
    - 26
    p: null
  assay:
    text: RNA-Seq
    term: EFO:0008896
    quoted:
    - 21
    p: 1.0
  target:
    na: RNA-Seq has no pull-down target
    p: 1.0
  control_type:
    na: Untreated samples are baseline, not control libraries
    p: 1.0
  # ... the other shared claims cut
samples:
  GSM3056966:
    biosample_accession: SAMN08742201
    biosample:
      id: B1
      inferred: no text read ties this library's material to another's
      p: null
    dose:
      text: 0 ug/ml
      value: 0
      unit: ug/ml
      level: 0_ug_ml
      quoted:
      - 5
      p: 1.0
    # ... the sample's other claims, and the other 22 samples, cut

Read it from the samples outward:

  • Sample GSM3056966 got a dose of 0 ug/ml. Passage 5 quotes the words from its GEO record, and its level on the factor dose is 0_ug_ml.
  • The factor dose says the study varied the dose on purpose, in three ordered levels, and compared the others with 0_ug_ml.
  • The claims under shared hold for every sample: each is human, and each library is RNA-Seq, RNA sequencing. target and control_type do not apply, so each is marked na.
  • Each p is the chance that the claim is right, as Jev judged it. Jev is a model that answers yes-or-no and multiple-choice questions with a probability.
  • biosample_accession is the sample's id in BioSample, the archive of sample records.

docs.title: Where the files are
docs.text:
File What it is <folder>/<ID>/reading.yaml A study's reading. seqforge study write-reading --out <folder> writes one per study from the reading pass's answers. seqforge study run runs that pass and that write after the bounds, and calls models through the model gateway. evals/standard-set/<ID>/job-reading.yaml The reading that the reading job wrote for each of the 50 studies of the standard set, written with study write-reading --name job-reading.yaml. evals/standard-set/<ID>/reading.yaml A reading worked by hand, for five studies of the standard set: GSE100021, GSE112068, GSE117724, GSE235532 and GSE241718.

<ID> is the study's name, such as GSE112068. study write-reading never overwrites a file that is already there. It writes no file for a study that the job refused, and it writes no text that the format check rejects.

Two commands read one file. Neither needs a model or a network.

seqforge study check-reading reading.yaml
seqforge study relations reading.yaml

The first command checks the file against this page. See The check. The second command prints what the reading implies between its samples, such as replicates and contrasts. See The relations.

seqforge run --study <folder> joins a reading into the compiler's sample table, sample_metadata.tsv. It matches each reading row to a compiled sample by biosample_accession.

docs.title: The file at a glance
docs.text:
A reading file has five parts. The arrows show how one part points at another.

flowchart TD
    HEAD["<b>header</b><br/><code>format</code> · <code>study</code><br/><code>models</code> · <code>read</code><br/><code>ontology_snapshot</code><br/><i>which study, who wrote it,<br/>what was read, where ids came from</i>"]
    SHARED["<b>shared</b><br/>the claims every sample has"]
    SAMPLES["<span style='color:#fff'><b>samples</b><br/>one row per sequenced sample:<br/>the claims of its own</span>"]
    FACTORS["<b>factors</b><br/>the labels the study varied:<br/>levels, baseline, ordered or not"]
    PASSAGES["<b>passages</b><br/>the numbered quotes,<br/>each with where it was read"]
    SRC[("GEO records<br/>and papers")]

    HEAD ~~~ SHARED
    SHARED -->|"a row's claim replaces<br/>the shared claim"| SAMPLES
    SAMPLES -->|"<code>level</code> names one<br/>of the factor's levels"| FACTORS
    SHARED -->|"<code>quoted</code>, <code>see</code> and<br/><code>against</code> list passage numbers"| PASSAGES
    SAMPLES --> PASSAGES
    FACTORS --> PASSAGES
    PASSAGES -->|"<code>record</code> or <code>paper</code>"| SRC

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class SAMPLES artifact

A sample's claims are its own row plus whatever shared adds. A claim that a source backs gives passage numbers, and each passage names the record or the paper that holds the quote. A claim that a source contradicts names that passage too, under against. A claim on a label that the study varied also names its level.

docs.title: The fields
docs.text:
Every field below is required unless the table says otherwise. The check rejects a file with any other top-level field.

Field Holds format The whole number 2. See When the format changes. study The study's name: the GEO Series it was picked by, such as GSE100021. It cannot be empty. models Who wrote the file. reading is the model that read the study. probabilities is the model that gave the p values. Either may be null. read What the model read: one or more of records, abstract and full_text. No other word is accepted. read_detail Optional. One sentence that says which records and which papers were read. ontology_snapshot Where the file's ontology ids came from. See The ontology snapshot. passages The quotes that back the claims, each under its number. It may be empty: {}. factors The labels that the study varied on purpose, each under its label. It may be empty: {}. shared The claims that every sample has unless its own row says otherwise. It may be empty: {}. samples One row per sequenced sample, each under the sample's id, such as GSM2668015. At least one.

The reading job writes read from what it had: always records, then abstract when a paper's abstract or full text was read, then full_text when a paper's full text was read.

docs.title: The ontology snapshot
docs.text:
An ontology is a published list of terms, each with an id, such as UBERON for anatomy. ontology_snapshot names, once for the whole file, where the file's ontology ids came from.

Field Holds source The dated snapshot of the ontologies, or the service that the ids were looked up in. It cannot be blank. date Its date, written as a date such as 2026-11-21.
  • ontology_snapshot is required when any claim has a term. A term on sex does not count, because a sex term is one of this page's own words and not an ontology id.
  • For ids from liulab-data's ontology store, date is the UTC day that the pass opened the store, which pinned its snapshots for the pass. liulab-data is the lab's package for archive records, papers and ontologies.

docs.title: Passages
docs.text:
A quote is written once in the file, however many claims it backs. passages is keyed by number, a whole number of 1 or more. Each passage holds the quote and where it was read, in one of two ways.

Field Holds quote The words, copied from the source as one unbroken span. It cannot be empty. record and field For a quote from a GEO record: the record, and the field of it. paper and section For a quote from a paper: the paper, written pmid:<number>, and the section of it.

A passage has record and field, or it has paper and section. The check rejects a passage with only one of a pair, or with parts of both.

record takes one of three forms:

  • one record id, such as GSE100021 or GSM2668015;
  • a list of record ids, when each of those records holds the quote in that field;
  • the word each_sample, when every sample record of the study holds the quote in that field.

A record quote is exact: the field holds it character for character. A paper's text comes with markup and broken lines. So a paper quote is exact after the markup is removed and each run of white space is collapsed to one space. A paper's section is where the quote was found: title, abstract, or a section of the full text.

The format check does not look for a quote in its source. The reading job finds every quote in its record or paper when it writes the file, and it drops a quote that it cannot find. Jev then judges whether each found passage backs its claim or speaks against it.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
A claim is one label of one sample: what the label's value is, how that is backed, and how sure the model is. In the short example, the dose entry of GSM3056966 is one claim.

Field Holds text The value, in the source's own words. term An ontology id for the value, such as UBERON:0002107. Written only when the match is clear. On treatment only, a list of ids when one sample got several compounds. value For an age, a dose, a duration or a label of the study's own: the number, or a range written [low, high]. YAML reads 1.7e12 as text, so write 1.7e+12. unit The unit of value, as a short text such as month, day, hour or ug/ml. level On a label that is a factor: the name of the sample's level. See Factors. id On biosample and donor: a short name made up in the file, such as B1. quoted Backing mark. A source says it. The mark lists the numbers of the passages that say so. inferred Backing mark. No passage says it outright. The mark is a short text that says how it was worked out. unknown Backing mark. What was read does not say. The mark is a short note. na Backing mark. The label does not apply to this sample. The mark is a short text that says why. see Optional, and never beside quoted. The numbers of the passages that the claim rests on. against Optional, beside any backing mark. The numbers of the passages that say otherwise. p A number from 0 to 1, or null. Required.

Only p and one backing mark are required. The check rejects a claim with any other field.

docs.title: The rules for a claim
docs.text:
• It has exactly one of quoted, inferred, unknown and na. The check rejects a claim with none, and a claim with two.
  • quoted lists at least one passage.
  • Every number in quoted, in see and in against must be a passage in the file.
  • The text after inferred, unknown or na cannot be blank.
  • A quoted claim and an inferred claim say something: each has text or value. A biosample claim and a donor claim may have an id and neither of the two.
  • An unknown claim and an na claim give no value. So neither has text, term, value, unit or level.
  • A term list is allowed only on treatment, and it cannot be empty.
  • A value has the type that this page writes for it. The check rejects a number in quotes, such as p: "0.5", and true where a number belongs.

docs.title: Which backing mark
docs.text:
The four backing marks answer three questions in turn:

flowchart LR
    A(["Does the label apply<br/>to this sample?"])
    B(["Can its value be told<br/>from what was read?"])
    C(["Does a passage<br/>say it outright?"])
    NA["<b><code>na</code></b><br/>why it does not apply<br/><i>no value</i>"]
    UNK["<b><code>unknown</code></b><br/>a short note<br/><i>no value</i>"]
    Q["<span style='color:#fff'><b><code>quoted</code></b><br/>the passage numbers<br/><i>has a value</i></span>"]
    I["<span style='color:#fff'><b><code>inferred</code></b><br/>how it was worked out<br/><i>has a value</i></span>"]

    A -->|yes| B
    A -->|no| NA
    B -->|yes| C
    B -->|no| UNK
    C -->|yes| Q
    C -->|no| I

    %% The inline white <span> is required on dark fills — see the comment in docs/index.md.
    classDef artifact fill:#00695c,stroke:#004d40
    class Q,I artifact

unknown and na are different gaps. unknown means that the label has a value and nothing that was read gives it. na means that the label has no value for this sample, such as the cell line of a tissue sample.

docs.title: When the sources disagree
docs.text:
against is for sources that disagree. Say the records give one value and the paper another. The claim writes the value that it judges right and backs it as usual. Then it lists the passages that say otherwise under against. Its p is the chance that the value it wrote is the right one.

A passage that the claim merely does not use is not against it: against names a contradiction. A factor is a claim, so a factor can have against too.

docs.title: What p means
docs.text:
p is the chance that the claim as written is right, given what read lists. A model judged it.

  • On an unknown claim, p is the chance that what was read really does not say.
  • null means that no model has given a probability yet. It does not mean that the claim is in doubt.
  • When any claim has a number, models.probabilities must name the model that gave it.

A bounds file writes its claims and its passages the same way.

docs.title: Samples and shared claims
docs.text:
Each row under samples holds the claims of one sample, each under its label. shared holds claims in the same form.

A shared claim stands for every sample. A sample has every claim under shared, except for a label that its own row writes. The row's claim replaces the shared claim whole: no field of the shared claim carries over. The reading job moves a claim that is the same on every sample, its p aside, under shared, and gives it the smallest of the samples' p. It never moves biosample, and it leaves shared empty for a study of one sample.

docs.title: The BioSample accession
docs.text:
A row can also hold one field that is not a claim: biosample_accession. It is the BioSample accession that the sample's GEO record links, such as SAMN08742201.

  • It is copied from the record and not read from any text. So it has no backing mark and no p.
  • It is written as SAMN, SAMEA or SAMD followed by digits: the accession forms of NCBI, of EMBL-EBI and of DDBJ, the three archives that share BioSample records.
  • It is absent when the record links no BioSample, and also when the record links more than one: an accession is copied, never chosen.
  • It is never under shared.
  • seqforge run --study joins the reading into sample_metadata.tsv by this accession.

Do not confuse it with the biosample label below, whose id is a name made up in the file.

docs.title: The 18 labels
docs.text:
Once the shared claims are applied, every sample must have all 18 labels below. A gap is written as unknown or na. So a label that is absent was forgotten, and the check rejects it.

Label Holds biosample The piece of material that the library was made from. Its id is required. Two samples with one id were made from the same material. donor The person or animal that the material came from. Its id names the individual. na when the material is a pool or has no single individual. assay The kind of sequencing experiment, such as RNA-Seq or ChIP-Seq. Term: EFO, the Experimental Factor Ontology, such as EFO:0008896 for RNA-Seq. target What a pull-down enriches: a histone mark or a protein. na for an assay with no pull-down, and for a control library. No term. Never a factor. control_type The kind of background-control library, such as input or IgG. na for every other library. species The species. Term: NCBI Taxonomy, written NCBITaxon:9606. Must be quoted or inferred. sex The sex. Term: one of female, male, hermaphrodite and mixed. age The age, with value and unit. development_stage The stage of life, such as fetal, larval or adult. Term: the stage list of the species: HsapDv for human, MmusDv for mouse, WBls for C. elegans, FBdv for the fruit fly. Any other species, such as the rat, has no stage list and no term. tissue The tissue or organ. Term: UBERON, or WBbt for C. elegans. cell_type The cell type. Term: Cell Ontology (CL). cell_line The cell line. Term: Cellosaurus. disease The disease or disease model. Term: MONDO, or PATO:0000461 for healthy. genotype The genotype, as text. strain The strain, as text. treatment What was applied to the sample. Term: ChEBI for a chemical, or a list of ChEBI ids when one sample got several compounds. A protein keeps its text with no term. dose How much of the treatment, with value and unit for one number. Text alone when no single number applies, such as "per side". duration How long the treatment was applied, with value and unit for one number. Text alone when no single number applies, such as "overnight".

Tissue, cell type and cell line are three labels, and a sample can have a value in each.

In the reading job, code writes three labels and the model writes none of them: biosample, donor and species. Code takes the species from the record's taxonomy id. Code also maps the text healthy to PATO:0000461.

A row or shared may hold more labels than the 18. Such a label is an attribute of the study's own, such as time_point in GSE112068 or a harvest time. Its claim has the same form.

docs.title: What the labels mean
docs.text:
Four points of meaning matter when you write or read these labels. The check does not test them.

  • control_type is about background-control libraries only. An input library or an IgG library measures the background of a pull-down. An untreated or wild-type group that the study compares the others with is a comparison baseline, not a control. Its control_type is na, and the factor's baseline names it.
  • duration is the length of the treatment itself. Any other time is an attribute of the study's own. The time from the end of a treatment to the harvest is one example.
  • An untreated sample in a study that treats writes its text. Its treatment says what it got, such as "untreated" or "vehicle (PBS)", and is not na. na on treatment is for a study with no treatment. The route, the side and what a time is measured from stay in text.
  • A pull-down library and its control are tied by the biosample id. No other field ties them. In the example with every part, each input has the id of the pull-down made from the same chromatin. This tie has a known limit. One control library that serves pull-downs made from different material cannot be tied to all of them, because the control has one biosample id.

docs.title: Which labels take a term or a value
docs.text:
• A sex term is one of the four words female, male, hermaphrodite and mixed.
  • Any other term is an id from the vocabulary that the table above names for the label and the sample's species. Examples are UBERON:0002107 for a mouse tissue and WBbt:0005772 for a worm tissue. A shared claim must fit the species of each sample that it stands for. On disease, PATO:0000461 for healthy is allowed too.
  • A label for which the table names no vocabulary takes no term. These are target, control_type, genotype, strain, age, dose and duration, a development_stage of a species with no stage list, and a label of the study's own.
  • Only age, dose, duration and a label of the study's own take a value.

The check judges each id by the vocabularies that liulab-data keeps. So check-reading needs liulab-data installed. Without it, the command exits 2 and prints no verdict.

docs.title: Factors
docs.text:
A factor is a label that the study varied on purpose, such as the treatment in a drug study or the age in an aging study. factors is keyed by that label. A sample's value is written once, in the sample's claim on the label. The factor adds the list of levels and how they compare.

Field Holds levels The names of the levels, at least one, each a short text. For an ordered factor, the order of this list is the order of the levels. baseline The level that the study compares the others with. null when the study compares the levels with each other and none is a reference, such as two tissues. Required. ordered true when the levels run along a scale, such as a time course or a dose series. Otherwise false. a backing mark, see, against, p A factor is a claim too. It is backed by quoted, inferred or unknown, never na.

The rules for a factor:

  • Its label must be a label of every sample. Where the label does not apply to a sample, the sample's claim on it is na.
  • baseline is one of levels, or null.
  • No level is named twice. A level name is text, so quote a name that YAML reads as a number: "0".
  • At least one sample is at each level in levels.
  • A sample's claim on the factor's label names its level in level, with one of the names in levels. Two samples with different text and the same level are at the same level.
  • A claim with no level on a factor's label means that the factor does not cover that sample. An example is a study that varied the genotype among its RNA-Seq samples only.
  • When the claim under shared names a level, a row's claim that replaces it names a level too. A row's claim that is unknown or na is the exception, because it names none.
  • The check rejects level on a label that is not a factor.
  • target is never a factor. The relations already keep samples with different targets apart, and a target has no baseline. The check rejects a factor keyed target.

docs.title: An example with every part
docs.text:
A liver study of two ages. Each age has one pull-down library and the input library made from the same chromatin. The paper gives the old mice a different age from the records.

format: 2
study: GSE900001
models:
  reading: example/model-a
  probabilities: example/model-b
read: [records, abstract]
read_detail: The Series, its four samples, and the abstract of the one paper.
ontology_snapshot: {source: example ontology snapshot, date: 2026-11-21}

passages:
  1: {record: GSE900001, field: Series_overall_design, quote: "H3K27me3 ChIP-seq and input from liver of young and old male mice"}
  2: {record: each_sample, field: Sample_organism_ch1, quote: "Mus musculus"}
  3: {record: [GSM9000001, GSM9000002], field: Sample_characteristics_ch1, quote: "age: 2 months"}
  4: {record: [GSM9000003, GSM9000004], field: Sample_characteristics_ch1, quote: "age: 24 months"}

factors:
  age:
    levels: [young, old]
    baseline: young

    p: 0.97

  donor:             {unknown: "No record says which animal a library came from", p: 0.8}

  target:            {text: H3K27me3, quoted: [1], p: 0.98}

  sex:               {text: male, term: male, quoted: [1], p: 0.97}
  development_stage: {text: adult, inferred: "A mouse of 2 months or more is an adult", see: [3, 4], p: 0.9}

samples:

    biosample:    {id: B1, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 2 months, value: 2, unit: month, level: young, quoted: [3], p: 0.97}
  GSM9000002:
    biosample:    {id: B1, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 2 months, value: 2, unit: month, level: young, quoted: [3], p: 0.97}
    target:       {na: "Input chromatin, no pull-down", p: 0.98}
    control_type: {text: input, quoted: [5], p: 0.98}
  GSM9000003:
    biosample:    {id: B2, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 24 months, value: 24, unit: month, level: old, quoted: [4], against: [7], p: 0.9}
  GSM9000004:
    biosample:    {id: B2, inferred: "One chromatin prep per age gave the pull-down and the input", see: [1], p: 0.7}
    age:          {text: 24 months, value: 24, unit: month, level: old, quoted: [4], against: [7], p: 0.9}

This example is made up to show every part. Its records, quotes, numbers and model names are not real. It passes the check.

  • The two input rows replace the shared target and the shared control_type.
  • The two old samples quote the records' age, 24 months, and name passage 7 under against, because the paper says 22 months.
  • time_of_day is a label of the study's own.

docs.title: The check
docs.text:
seqforge study check-reading <file> reads one file and prints one JSON object:

{
  "file": "reading.yaml",
  "format": 2,
  "valid": false,
  "problems": [
    {"field": "samples.GSM9000003.strain", "reason": "missing: every sample has this label, in its own row or under shared"},
    {"field": "shared.assay.quoted", "reason": "passage 7 does not exist"}
  ]
}

file is the path you gave. format is the format number that the check accepts. Each problem names the field and the reason. samples.GSM9000003.strain is the strain claim of that sample.

Exit code Meaning 0 The file is valid. 3 The file is rejected. problems lists why. 2 The file cannot be read, or liulab-data is not installed. A file that is not UTF-8 text cannot be read.

The check also rejects these, each with exit code 3:

  • Text that is not YAML, or YAML that is not a mapping of fields. The problem's field is (file).
  • A wrong or missing format. The check asks about the format number first, and alone. A file with another number gets that one problem, which names the number that the check expected.
  • A key that one mapping writes twice. The problem names the key. Plain YAML keeps the last of the two and reports nothing, so a second row for one sample would replace the first unseen.

The check asks only whether the file is well formed. It reads the file alone and opens no record. So it does not look for a quote in its source, and it does not judge whether a claim is right.

docs.title: The relations
docs.text:
A reading does not store which samples are replicates or which groups the study contrasts. Those follow from the claims. So seqforge study relations <file> works them out on every run and writes no file. The command checks the file first, and it rejects a broken file exactly as check-reading does. For a valid file, the JSON object has one more field, relations.

These terms define the relations:

  • Two samples have the same assay, the same target or the same control type when the two claims have the same text, or are both na, or are both unknown.
  • A group is the set of samples that have the same assay, target, control type and level on every factor. A group can be one sample.
  • A control library is a sample whose control_type claim is quoted or inferred. A sample whose control type is unknown is not a control library.
  • A signal is a sample whose target claim is quoted or inferred and that is not a control library.
Relation Holds replicates Each group of two or more samples: the same assay, target, control type and level on every factor. Each entry gives the assay, target, control_type, the levels on every factor, and the samples. contrasts Each pair of groups that have the same assay, target and control type, and differ in the level of exactly one factor. Neither group is a control library. One of the two is at the factor's baseline. For a factor with a null baseline, each pair of levels is one contrast. series For each ordered factor: the samples in level order, among the samples that have the same assay, target, control type and level on every other factor. So input libraries and IgG libraries never share a series. A series has at least two levels. shared_biosample Each set of two or more samples with one biosample id. signal_to_control Within one such set: each signal, paired with each control library.

For the example with every part, the command prints the relations below. Samples, factors and levels are listed in the file's order. The picture shows the same relations, and the JSON follows it.

  • In a contrast, levels holds the two levels, with the baseline first when the factor has one.
  • fixed holds the level of every other factor, which the two groups share.
  • A null assay, target or control type means that the claim is na or unknown.
  • A null level means that the factor does not cover those samples.

docs.title: When the format changes
docs.text:
There is one format at a time. format is a whole number, and the check accepts only the current one. A file with another number is rejected, and the message names the number that the check expected.

A change to the format raises the number and rewrites every existing file in the same change. No file stays behind in an older format. Git history is the only record of the old form.

docs.title: Read your own studies
docs.text:
This guide takes a list of GEO Series (studies in the Gene Expression Omnibus archive) and gives you two files for each study, plus a report page:

  • bounds.yaml says which Series and which papers belong to the study, and which linked records were left out and why.
  • reading.yaml says what each sequenced sample was: its species, tissue or cell type, condition, and the factors the study varied on purpose, such as a treatment or an age. Each statement quotes the record or paper it came from, or says that it was inferred or unknown.

Models draw the bounds and write the reading. Code checks each quote against its source and each file against its format before it writes the file. To see what the result looks like, open the example reports. Understanding a study explains how the two models work and why a study can end unsettled.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need seqforge with liulab-data installed (see Getting started), and these four settings in your shell:

Variable What it points at Needed for LABLLM_GATEWAY The lab's model gateway, as http://host:port. Open a tunnel to it first Every model question. Without it the run stops before it spends anything LABDATA_STORE liulab-data's record store: its local copy of GEO and SRA records Finding each study's linked Series, samples and papers LABDATA_PAPERS liulab-data's paper store Reading a study's papers. A study that has a paper waits until this is set LABDATA_ONTOLOGIES liulab-data's ontology store: dated lists of terms for species, tissues, cell types and conditions Naming each value in the reading by an ontology term

If you saved a store's location with liulab-data itself, you can leave its variable unset. Reach the lab gateway says how to open the tunnel.

docs.title: Set up a folder of studies
docs.text:
Make an empty folder for the studies. seqforge makes one folder in it for each study, named by its Series id. List the studies in one of two ways.

A pick.yaml in the folder. It needs a studies list, with the Series id of each study under id:

studies:
  - id: GSE100021
  - id: GSE126954
  - id: GSE140511

A keys file. Write one Series id on each line, and pass the file with --keys. A keys file overrides the folder's pick.yaml, and the run takes the studies in the file's order.

GSE100021
GSE126954

Each id must be a GEO Series, GSE and a number. Start from the Series the study was published under. The bounding job finds the other Series and papers linked to it.

docs.title: Run it under a spending limit
docs.text:
Pick one working folder and run every command from it. seqforge keeps the record of each pass in seqforge/passes/ under the folder you run from, and a rerun from the same place resumes it.

seqforge study run --studies <folder> --ceiling-usd 2

--ceiling-usd is required and has no default. It is the most both jobs together may spend, in dollars. The bounding job spends first, and the reading job gets what is left. To run only some studies, add --keys <file>.

The command runs four steps in order:

  1. The bounding job asks a model about each linked record.
  2. seqforge writes <folder>/<ID>/bounds.yaml for each study.
  3. The reading job reads the records and papers that the bounds kept.
  4. seqforge writes <folder>/<ID>/reading.yaml for each study.

It prints one JSON object. spent_usd is what the run paid, and steps holds what each step printed. The first step that fails stops the run.

docs.title: What a run costs
docs.text:
The bounding job asks Jev, a model that answers yes-or-no and multiple-choice questions with a probability. The reading job asks Jev and a writer model, DeepSeek Flash, which lists each study's factors and values. To use another model for one of these roles, pass --model.

A first run costs a few cents a study, nearly all of it for the reading. The gateway keeps every answer, so a rerun of the same studies pays nothing. How many studies a run can take at once is --units-at-once (32 by default). Each run of the standard set, the lab's fixed list of 50 small GEO studies, is measured in a dated note with its cost and time; the latest is the study chain on the 50 studies.

docs.title: Read how each study ended
docs.text:
Each job ends each study in one of three ways.

Ending What it means File written Settled Every check passed. Yes Unsettled The file passed its checks, but Jev was asked a question twice, in two forms, and the two answers did not agree, or Jev left a question unanswered. A person or a stronger model should look at it Yes Refused The job could not give an answer it could check. The reason says why, such as a group of more than 50 linked Series, or a writer answer that could not be used twice No

For bounding, Jev is asked about each record twice: as written, and negated. For reading, Jev is asked twice whether each factor was varied on purpose, which level is the baseline, and each sample's level. Any disagreement makes the study unsettled.

The ending is kept in the pass's record, not in the study's files. You can find it in two places:

  • In the JSON that study run prints, the two write steps list each study under studies, with its ending. A refused study has its reason there.
  • seqforge pass status study-bounds and seqforge pass status study-reading print the count of each ending. Run them from the same working folder. They work while a pass runs and with the gateway down.

A study can also wait without an ending. That happens when its id is not a GEO Series, when the record store does not hold it, when it has a paper and no paper store is set, or, for the reading, when its bounds.yaml is missing or fails its check. pass status lists each waiting study under not_done, with the reason. Fix the reason, then run again.

docs.title: Resume a run that stopped
docs.text:
Run the same command again. A study that was already answered replays from the gateway's cache and costs nothing, so the rerun pays only for studies not yet answered.

The exit code says why a run stopped:

Code Meaning 0 Every step finished. Some studies may still be unsettled or refused 2 It could not start, such as no gateway or a store it cannot open. Nothing was spent 3 It stopped: at the spending limit, at a provider's limit, while another process held the pass, or at a file that failed its format check

A file already on disk is never replaced. To take a newer answer for a study, delete its file first, then run again.

docs.title: Check a file
docs.text:
Each file has a format, and a check that seqforge runs before it writes the file. You can run the same check on any file, for example one you edited by hand:

seqforge study check-bounds <folder>/<ID>/bounds.yaml
seqforge study check-reading <folder>/<ID>/reading.yaml

Each prints valid and a list of problems, each naming a field and the reason. The exit code is 0 for a valid file, 3 for a file with problems, and 2 for a file it cannot read. check-reading needs liulab-data installed, because it checks that each ontology id comes from the vocabulary its label uses, such as UBERON: for a tissue. It does not look the term itself up, and it checks the file alone, so it does not look the quotes up in their records either. The format pages list every field: the bounds file and the reading file.

docs.title: Make a report for a study
docs.text:
seqforge report --study <folder>/<ID>

This writes report.html and report.json into the study's folder. The page opens in any browser with no network. It shows the bounds as a graph of the records kept and left out, and the reading's samples in tables by topic. It does not show whether the job ended the study settled or unsettled. That is in the pass's record, as described above.

To join a reading to a compiled dataset, pass the same study folder to seqforge run --study when you compile. From FASTQ files to a pipeline explains the join.

docs.text:
