  • Passes covers running one job at a time, its spending limit, and what a pass prints.

docs.title: From FASTQ files to a pipeline
docs.text:
The compiler turns a set of FASTQ files into a pipeline you can run. It works like a compiler for code: you hand it source, it checks the source, and it writes a program. Here the source is your sequencing files and what you know about them, and the program is a Snakemake workflow (a Snakefile and its settings). seqforge writes the pipeline. You submit it. seqforge never submits a job.

This page explains what happens on the way. To do it yourself, see Compile step by step or Compile with Claude. Each command's options are in the command reference.

docs.title: What goes in
docs.text: Input Needed? What it is for FASTQ files (.fastq.gz) Yes The bytes decide what kind of library this is. The genome Yes A genome assembly by its UCSC id (the assembly's name in the UCSC Genome Browser), such as ce11, and a named gene annotation. This is the one choice with no safe default, so seqforge asks for it. An archive accession No The archive's records for each sample, such as an SRA project. Most sequencing data never had one. Papers and notes No A paper (.pdf, .txt or .md) or a supplementary .xlsx table. A model reads it for claims about the library. You can skip this step and use no model at all. Instructions No A document written for seqforge, such as "count introns too". Only this kind of document can change what to do with the data.

docs.title: What comes out
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["FASTQ files"] --> M["manifest.yaml<br/>what the data is"]
    A["records and papers<br/>(optional)"] --> M
    M --> C["compose"]
    P["processing.yaml<br/>what to do with it"] --> C
    C --> S["Snakefile<br/>you submit it"]
  • The manifest (manifest.yaml) says what the data is: the library type, how each file's reads are laid out, the organism and the samples. There is one per dataset.
  • The recipe (processing.yaml) says what to do with it: the genome, the aligner, what to count and the computing environment. There can be many per dataset.
  • The pipeline is a folder that holds the Snakefile, its settings, and a table that says where every FASTQ file is and which sample and read it belongs to.
  • The sample table (sample_metadata.tsv) has one row per sample.

All of it goes into a seqforge/ folder in your project. Only seqforge/cache/ is safe to delete.

docs.title: How the library type is found from the bytes
Filenames are not evidence
docs.text: _1 and _2 in a file name come from whatever wrote the file: an archive's download tool, a sequencer's demultiplexer, or a script. SRR123_1.fastq.gz is not "read 1" in any biological sense. It might hold the cell barcodes, the RNA, or nothing useful. So seqforge opens the files and looks.

docs.title: It reads only the start of each file
docs.text:
Every look at a FASTQ file is bounded. By default seqforge reads the first 2,000 reads, and never more than 256 MB once decompressed, whichever comes first. You can raise the read count to sample more of a large file, but the limit always applies. Reading a whole multi-gigabyte file is treated as a bug, even when today's file is small. The limits are in reads and bytes, never in seconds, because time depends on the disk and on how busy the machine is.

From that bounded start, the bytes tell a lot:

  • Which positions are fixed and which vary. The same base at one position in almost every read is adapter sequence, not data. A long run of T is a poly-T tail.
  • Which stretches repeat. Cell barcodes recur, because each cell is sequenced many times. UMIs (unique molecular identifiers) and RNA are nearly all distinct. This tells barcodes from UMIs without any barcode list.
  • Whether someone trimmed the file before upload. A sequencing run writes its technical reads at one fixed length. If most reads of such a read are another length, a trimming tool ran, and trimming tools do not know a barcode from an adapter. seqforge refuses such a file instead of reading barcodes from shifted positions.

docs.title: The knowledge base says what each technology looks like
docs.text:
The knowledge base holds one entry for each supported technology, such as 10x Chromium 3' v3 or SPLiT-seq. An entry states what the technology's files hold: for example, one 28-base read with a cell barcode and a UMI, and one read of RNA. It also states the strand and the barcode list. Each entry carries its own test, which proves that the entry finds its own technology again. The knowledge base lists the supported assays.

seqforge scores every entry against the bytes. For each one, it tries every way of matching your files to the entry's reads and keeps the best match. A swapped _1 and _2 gives the same answer.

docs.title: Cheap checks come first
docs.text:
Answers are tried in order of cost, and seqforge climbs only as far as it has to:

Step What it uses How much it counts 0 The prose: a paper or record that says "10x 3' v3" A hint that says which list to check first. Never a conclusion. 1 The filenames A weak hint, never decisive. 2 The shape of the reads: lengths, fixed and varying positions, repeats Strong. The bytes are being read anyway. 3 One barcode list: do these barcodes appear in the vendor's list of real barcodes? Strong. 7 A person Asked only when two technologies tie and would process the reads differently.

A tie that survives step 3 and would change the output goes to a person as a question. A tie that would not change the output, such as 10x 3' v3 against v3.1, records both names and asks nothing.

The prose sits at the bottom on purpose. A paper that says "10x v3" turns an open search into a yes-or-no check of one barcode list. It is trusted enough to skip the search, never enough to skip the check. When the prose and the bytes disagree, seqforge reports the disagreement, and the bytes win (see why you can trust the output).

docs.title: Which file is which sample comes from the records
docs.text: Which sample each file belongs to comes from the archive records, not from the bytes. A disagreement there, such as a file whose size differs from what the archive says, is a warning and does not stop the compile.

docs.title: The manifest: what the data is
docs.text:
The manifest records facts about data that already exists. The molecules went through the sequencer and produced those bytes, and nothing you decide later changes that.

  • One per dataset. A dataset here means one technology. A project that mixes technologies, such as 10x v2 and v3 libraries in one Series, splits into assays, one per technology, decided from the bytes. Each assay gets its own manifest and pipeline under seqforge/<assay>/, and project.yaml lists them. A sample whose files disagree on technology stops the compile.
  • Named by its hash. A hash is a short fingerprint computed from the content. The manifest's hash is computed from what it says about the library and the experiment. The same data gives the same hash, on any machine.
  • Written once. A finished manifest is never rewritten when you change your mind about processing.
  • No machine paths. The genome is a UCSC id plus a registered annotation name, software is a named environment, and data is a web or archive address. The manifest means the same thing on any machine.

docs.title: The recipe: what to do with it
docs.text:
The recipe holds the choices: which genome build, which aligner, what to count. Someone else could choose differently, and you may choose differently next year. So the recipe is a separate file, and a dataset can have many recipes. Changing a recipe never changes the dataset's hash.

The line between the two files is between parsing and counting:

  • How to parse the reads (where the barcode starts, how long the UMI is, which strand) is a fact of the technology. The bytes and the knowledge base decide it. No instruction and no paper can set it, because the recipe has no field for it.
  • What to count (genes only, or genes plus introns, against which genome) is a choice. It lives in the recipe, and you can set it.

When several sources set the same recipe value, a command-line option wins over an instruction document, and an instruction wins over seqforge's default. An empty recipe is valid: every value then takes its default.

Some defaults avoid a question. Whether a 10x library came from whole cells or from nuclei cannot be read from the bytes, and it changes what to count. So for a droplet single-cell library the default recipe counts five ways in one pass: exons only, exons plus introns, two variants of that for reads that touch both, and spliced against unspliced reads. Alignment costs far more than counting, so the extra counts are close to free.

docs.title: The pipeline you submit
docs.text:
compose pairs one manifest with one recipe and writes a pipeline folder, seqforge/pipeline/<recipe>-<id>/. The id is computed from the dataset, the recipe, the knowledge base entry that decided the settings, and the version of the workflow module. Two recipes over one dataset therefore never write into the same folder, and every pipeline traces back to what made it. The same inputs always give the same pipeline.

The Snakefile uses hand-written, versioned Snakemake modules that ship with seqforge. No model writes pipeline code. You submit the Snakefile to your own machine or cluster. It ends in each sample's results, such as a count matrix per sample (<sample>.h5ad, the AnnData format) for single-cell RNA, or a fragments file for single-cell ATAC.

seqforge run does every step above in order and stops at the first refusal. Run it again and it resumes from what is already on disk.

docs.title: Joining a study's reading
docs.text:
The compiler knows which samples there are, their organism and their technology. It does not know what each sample was: its tissue, its treatment, its age. A study's reading holds that (see Understanding a study).

When you name a study folder with --study, the compile joins that folder's reading.yaml into sample_metadata.tsv. The two meet on the BioSample accession: the manifest sample's accession, and the biosample_accession that the reading's row copied from its GEO record. The table gains one column per factor and per label that varies across the samples, plus reading_hash, which names the reading it came from. A label that is the same for every sample tells no samples apart, so it gets no column.

The join never changes the manifest or its hash, and it never stops a compile. Each mismatch is a warning:

  • a compiled sample with no reading row, or one whose BioSample several rows link;
  • a reading row with no compiled sample;
  • a species that is not the manifest's organism;
  • an assay term that does not match the manifest's assay.

For a droplet library, the pipeline's last step copies these labels into each sample's .h5ad file. Without --study, nothing is joined.

docs.title: The report
docs.text: seqforge report writes one page, report.html, and its data, report.json, into the folder it starts from. For a compile, the page shows what seqforge decided and the evidence for it, and the pipeline's own results once it has run. With --study, it also shows the study's bounds, its design and its samples. The page opens in a browser with no network. The example reports show three.

docs.title: Understanding a study
docs.text:
A lab deposits its data in GEO, the Gene Expression Omnibus, as one or more Series. A Series is a deposit, not a piece of research. One paper's experiments can span several Series, and a Series rarely says in one place what each sample was. The study chain answers two questions for each study you give it:

  1. Its bounds. Which GEO Series and which papers are one piece of research?
  2. Its reading. What was each sample: which factors did the study vary on purpose, which level of each was each sample at, and what was it (its species, tissue, assay and so on)?

Each answer is a file in the study's folder: bounds.yaml, then reading.yaml. This page explains what the two files claim and how far to trust them. To run the chain yourself, see Read your own studies. For real output, see the example reports.

flowchart LR
    S["a GEO Series<br/>you start from"] --> B["bounding"]
    G["linked Series<br/>and papers"] --> B
    B --> BF["bounds.yaml<br/>which records are one study"]
    BF --> R["reading"]
    P["records, samples<br/>and papers"] --> R
    R --> RF["reading.yaml<br/>what each sample was"]

docs.title: The bounds say which records are one study
docs.text:
A study is one piece of research: the experiments that one paper reports, or one project that has no paper yet. A study is always made of whole Series. Nothing splits a Series by sample.

Bounding starts from one Series. It gathers that Series, every Series one link away from it, and every paper any of them links. Then it decides which of these belong:

  • Code keeps the starting Series. If the starting Series is a SuperSeries (a Series that only groups other Series), code keeps its sub-Series and leaves the SuperSeries itself out.
  • For every other Series and every paper, a model answers one question: does this record belong to the study? The model is Jev, which answers yes-or-no and multiple-choice questions with a probability.
  • Code copies the title of each record it placed, kept or left out, into the file.

A record that does not belong is listed as left out, with the reason. The bounding job reads each record's text and each paper's abstract, nothing more.

docs.title: The reading says what each sample was
docs.text:
The reading has one row for each sequenced sample of the kept Series. A sample that was not sequenced, such as a microarray sample, is left out. The reading holds three kinds of statement:

  • Factors. A factor is a label the study varied on purpose, such as a treatment or an age. The reading names the levels the factor took, the level the others are compared with (its baseline), and whether the levels have an order. Each sample's row names its level of each factor.
  • Labels. There are 18 standard labels, among them species, sex, age, tissue, cell type, cell line, disease, genotype, strain, treatment, dose, duration, assay and, for pull-down assays such as ChIP-seq, the target and the control type. A study can add a label of its own. A label that is the same for every sample is written once, under shared.
  • The BioSample accession. When a sample's GEO record links exactly one NCBI BioSample, the row copies its SAMN… id. This is an id copied from the record, not a claim. A compile uses it to join the reading to its samples (see From FASTQ files to a pipeline).

Two models write a reading. A writer model (DeepSeek Flash, with its reasoning mode on) reads the records and the papers. It lists the factors, every value each label takes, and a quote for each value. Jev then picks each sample's level and value from those lists. Papers are read in full when the lab's paper store holds the full text, and by their abstract otherwise.

Some facts follow from the labels, so no file stores them. Code works them out from a valid reading each time: which samples are replicates, which groups a comparison sets side by side, which samples run along an ordered factor, which libraries came from one piece of material, and which control goes with which pull-down.

docs.title: Every claim says how it is backed
docs.text:
Each statement in a study file is a claim. A claim carries exactly one mark that says how it is backed, and p, the chance it is right:

Mark What it means quoted A passage in a record or a paper says so. The claim lists the passage numbers. inferred No passage says so directly. The claim says how the value was reached. unknown What was read does not say. The claim carries a short note, and its p is the chance that the sources really do not say. na The label does not apply, such as a dose in a study with no treatment. Reading only.

A claim is quoted only after two checks pass. First, code finds the quote in its source. In a record, the quote must match the field character for character. In a paper, it must match once each run of spaces and line breaks counts as one space. Second, Jev reads the found passage beside the claim and judges whether the passage says so. A quote that code cannot find is dropped, so the claim can be at most inferred. A found passage that speaks against a claim is listed under against, so a reader sees the disagreement.

Labels such as tissue, cell type and disease also get an ontology term, a standard id from a public vocabulary. The terms come from the lab's ontology store. Its search offers candidates for each value, and Jev picks one or none. A term is written only when Jev's pick is at least 80% sure. The species comes from the taxonomy id in the sample's own record. The source's own words stay beside each term, and the file names the dated snapshot of the vocabularies that its ids came from.

docs.title: Each question is asked twice
docs.text:
A model's answer counts only where code can check it, and code decides whether it stands. In the study chain, the check is a second asking.

Jev answers a yes-or-no question with the chance of yes. Code reads that as yes above 0.5 and as no below. Each question that decides a study is asked twice:

  • A yes-or-no question is asked as written, then turned into its negation.
  • A multiple-choice question is asked with its options in order, then with the options reversed.

The two answers agree only when both lean the same way. A question that gets no answer never agrees. An answer that flips when the question is turned around is one the model was not sure of, whatever its probability said.

Bounding asks twice about every record it places. Reading asks twice about each factor (was it varied on purpose, and what is its baseline) and about each sample's level of each factor. A sample's other labels are asked once.

docs.title: A study ends settled, unsettled or refused
docs.text:
Ending Bounding Reading Settled Jev's two answers agree on every record. The two askings agree on every factor, baseline and level. Unsettled The two answers disagree on at least one record. The two askings disagree on at least one of those questions, or one went unanswered. Refused The linked group holds more than 50 Series, Jev gives no answer about a record, or the file fails its format check. The writer's answer cannot be used after one retry, the study has no sequenced sample, the writer lists more than 25 values for one label, or the file fails its format check.

A refused study gets no file. A settled or unsettled study gets a file that passes its format check. The ending is kept in the job's record of the run, not in the file, and the report does not show it. For an unsettled study, read the factors and levels with care: at least one of those answers changed when the question was turned around.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Every run takes a spending limit in dollars and stops when it reaches it. A model call made once is kept in the cache of the lab's model gateway, so a re-run of the same studies replays from it at no cost.

On the 50 studies of the standard set, a first run costs a few cents a study, nearly all of it for the reading. Each run of the 50 is measured in a dated note under docs/research/, with its cost and how each study ended; the latest is the study chain on the 50 studies.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It reads no sequencing data. The chain reads archive records and papers only. It opens no FASTQ file and no supplementary file.
  • It does not score itself. Settled means the two askings agreed. It does not mean the reading is right. Accuracy is measured by a separate effort, and nothing in the chain grades a reading.
  • It does not compile. A reading joins into a compile only when you name its study folder (see From FASTQ files to a pipeline).

The exact fields and rules of the two files are in the bounds file and the reading file. Each step in full is in the study workflow.

docs.title: Why you can trust the output
docs.text: A tool that always gives an answer is only as good as the person who checks it. Across thousands of public datasets, nobody checks every answer. So seqforge is built to stop where an ordinary pipeline would carry on, and to show the evidence for each answer it does give. This page lists the rules behind that, and then says plainly what seqforge does not promise.

docs.title: It refuses rather than guesses
docs.text:
A refusal is an exit code, the number a command returns when it ends, not a line in a log that nobody reads. A script or a person can act on it. Two codes are refusals: 3, blocked, when something is wrong with the data itself, and 4, a question that only a person can settle. Commands lists every code.

flowchart TD
    START["a dataset"] --> Q{"can code decide it?"}
    Q -->|yes| OK["manifest<br/>exit 0"]
    Q -->|"something is wrong<br/>with the data"| BLK["blocked<br/>exit 3"]
    Q -->|"a real question only<br/>a person can settle"| ASK["question<br/>exit 4"]

Each block carries a reason and a fix you can act on. "Could not process" is not a fix. "The barcode read is missing: download it again with the technical reads, or get the submitter's original files" is. Code decides whether a compile goes on. A model never does.

docs.title: It catches the quiet failures
docs.text:
Loud failures take care of themselves: a corrupt file crashes and you notice. Each failure below gives a normal-looking result, and an ordinary pipeline exits 0 on all of them.

  • A trimmed barcode file. A trimming tool ran before upload, so some barcodes sit at shifted positions. Those cells match no barcode list and drop out, and the matrix just looks thin. seqforge checks whether most reads of a fixed-length read have left that length, and refuses the file if they have.
  • Counting only exons on nuclei. Nuclei are full of unspliced RNA that sits in introns. Count only exons and you throw it away: 40.7% of one nuclear library, in a measurement on this project. The bytes of a nuclear library look the same as those of a whole-cell one. So for a droplet single-cell library, seqforge counts five ways in one pass, and you choose later.
  • The wrong genome. A worm library against the human genome barely maps, which is loud. The same mistake between two similar genomes is quiet, and gives a plausible matrix in the wrong coordinates. seqforge has no default genome. You name it.
  • The wrong strand. Map against the wrong strand and about half the reads go unassigned. Public records almost never state the strand. seqforge takes it from the technology's entry in the knowledge base, never from a guess.

docs.title: It asks only questions that matter
docs.text:
A tool that asks questions all the time is one people work around, and then it protects nobody. So seqforge does not ask in two cases:

  • The answer would change nothing. Two technology versions, such as 10x 3' v3 and v3.1, can look the same in the reads and also process the reads the same way. Then seqforge records both names and moves on.
  • Every answer is affordable. "Cells or nuclei?" cannot be answered from the reads, so seqforge counts every way at once instead of asking.

It asks only where the answers exclude each other: two technologies that tie and would process the reads differently.

docs.title: The bytes win over prose
docs.text:
Every judgement in the manifest says how it came to be known: read from the bytes (observed), claimed by a person, a paper or an archive (asserted), or worked out by code (inferred). A claim is never a measurement, however trusted its source.

A paper's statement of the library type is at most a hint about which barcode list to try first. It never counts as evidence. When the bytes and a record or paper disagree on a fact, seqforge does not pick a side quietly. It reports the disagreement, with both sides and where each came from, and stops at exit 4 until a person confirms.

docs.title: Every quote must be found in its source
docs.text:
A model that reads prose must quote the words that back each claim. Code then looks for the quote:

  • In the compiler, the quote must appear in the document, and it must carry the value. For a value from a fixed list, such as a technology name, the quote must name that technology. A claim that fails either check is rejected.
  • In the study chain, the quote must appear in its record field character for character, or in its paper once spaces and line breaks are evened out. A model then judges whether the found passage says what the claim says. A claim whose quote is not found is marked inferred, never quoted. See Understanding a study.

docs.title: A model answers only where code can check it
docs.text:
A model writes an answer only where code can check it, and code decides whether the answer stands.

  • No model writes code. The pipeline is built from hand-written, versioned modules. A model's output is data, and code checks it against a fixed format before using it.
  • In the compiler, one step uses a model: reading papers and records for claims. You can turn it off, and the manifest is still correct, only with less in it. The library type comes from the bytes either way.
  • In the study chain, models draw a study's bounds and write its reading. Code finds every quote, owns the threshold that turns a probability into yes or no, and asks each deciding question twice. An answer that flips when the question is turned around leaves the study unsettled.

A model never sets a threshold and never reads a technology from the bytes.

docs.title: Cheap checks first
docs.text:
seqforge tries the cheapest evidence first and climbs only on a real tie: the prose, then the filenames, then the shape of the reads, then one barcode list, and only then a person. The manifest records which step settled each decision. From FASTQ files to a pipeline walks through the steps.

It reads only a bounded start of each file, by default 2,000 reads or 256 MB decompressed, whichever comes first. It never reads a whole FASTQ file.

docs.title: The same answer on any machine
docs.text:
• No machine paths. The manifest names the genome by its UCSC id (the assembly's name in the UCSC Genome Browser) and a registered annotation name, the software by a named environment, and each file by its address. It means the same thing on your laptop and on a cluster.
  • Named by its hash. The manifest is named by a hash of what it says about the data. A new recipe never changes it, so a dataset keeps one name however many ways you process it.
  • Every step is saved. Each stage writes its result to disk. Run a command again and it resumes from what is there.

docs.title: What it does not promise
docs.text:
• A settled study is not a correct one. Settled means the two askings agreed. Accuracy is measured by a separate effort, against hand-checked files, and nothing in seqforge grades a reading.
  • A record can be wrong. Which file belongs to which sample, and a sample's BioSample link, come from the archive's records. seqforge warns where records disagree with each other or with the files, but it cannot correct a record that is wrong and consistent.
  • A claim can sit in the wrong field. The quote check catches an invented quote and a quote pinned to the wrong value from a fixed list. It cannot catch a real quote filed under the wrong free-text field. Such a claim never decides the library type, which comes from the bytes.
  • The pipeline still has to run. seqforge writes the Snakefile; you submit it. What the run measures comes back in the report as advice. It never changes a decision already recorded.

docs.title: Knowledge base
docs.text:
The knowledge base is how seqforge knows what a sequencing library is. It holds one entry per technology: the layout of each read, where the barcodes sit, and which barcode lists they come from. seqforge scores your files against every entry and picks the one the bytes match. That entry decides how your data is aligned.

You do not choose an entry. The bytes do. This page answers "is my assay supported?", and helps you read seqforge's answer when it tells you what your data is.

docs.title: Supported assays
docs.text: These are the technologies seqforge can compile today, from seqforge kb list. A barcode read is the read that carries the cell barcode and the UMI (unique molecular identifier, a random tag on each molecule). A barcode list is the published set of barcodes a chemistry can contain.

docs.title: Droplet single-cell RNA-seq from 10x Genomics
docs.text: Assay Entry How seqforge tells it apart Chromium 3' v3 and v3.1 10x-3p-gex-v3, 10x-3p-gex-v3.1 A 28 bp barcode read (16 bp barcode, 12 bp UMI) that hits the v3 barcode list. v3 and v3.1 are processed the same way, so seqforge records both names Chromium 3' v2 10x-3p-gex-v2 A 26 bp barcode read (16 bp barcode, 10 bp UMI) and its own barcode list GEM-X 3' v4 10x-gemx-3p-v4 The v3 read layout, with its own barcode list Chromium 5' v1 and v2 10x-5p-gex-v2 The same reads and barcode list as 3' v2. The paper or archive record must say 5' or 3' GEM-X 5' v3 10x-5p-gex-v3 The v3 read layout, with its own barcode list Multiome, gene expression arm 10x-multiome-gex The v3 read layout, with the Multiome barcode list Multiome, chromatin (ATAC) arm 10x-multiome-atac Three reads: two from the genome, and a barcode read of up to 24 bp holding a 16 bp barcode and no UMI. It gives a fragments file, not a count matrix

docs.title: Other single-cell RNA-seq
docs.text: Assay Entry How seqforge tells it apart BD Rhapsody WTA (whole transcriptome), original bead bd-rhapsody-wta Two fixed linker sequences at fixed places in the barcode read, and three barcode lists BD Rhapsody WTA, Enhanced bead bd-rhapsody-wta-enhanced-v1, bd-rhapsody-wta-enhanced-v2 Two short linkers after a 0 to 3 bp insert. The barcode lists tell the 96-label bead from the 384-label bead SPLiT-seq splitseq Two fixed 30 bp linkers in the barcode read, and three barcode lists, one per round Smart-seq3 smartseq3 One cell per file pair. Some reads start with an 11 bp tag, then an 8 bp UMI

docs.title: Bulk RNA-seq
docs.text:
Assay Entry How seqforge tells it apart Bulk RNA-seq bulk-rnaseq No barcode read at all. Paired-end or single-end

Each linked assay has its own page with its read layout and what goes wrong with it. The other entries have no page on this site yet. seqforge kb show <entry> prints any entry in full.

docs.title: How seqforge picks an entry
docs.text:
seqforge reads a bounded head of each file, 2,000 reads by default, and checks the cheapest evidence first. The number of reads and their lengths come first. Fixed sequences such as linkers come next. Barcode-list matches come last.

  • A family narrows to its members. Related chemistries form a family. The 10x 3' family is one loose pattern: a 16 bp barcode at the start of a 26 to 28 bp read. seqforge first places the data in the family, then picks the exact chemistry by read length and barcode list. So a vague mention in a paper, such as "10x 3'", still ends in an exact chemistry chosen from the bytes.
  • Two chemistries processed the same way are both recorded. 10x 3' v3 and v3.1 look the same in the reads and are aligned with the same settings. seqforge records both names and asks nothing.
  • Two chemistries processed differently must be told apart. Usually the barcode list settles it. When nothing in the reads can, as for 10x 3' v2 against 5' v1 and v2, seqforge turns to the paper or the archive record. If those do not settle it, it stops and asks you (exit code 4) rather than guessing.

A paper's claim about the chemistry is only a hint. It can break a tie the bytes cannot. If the paper and the bytes disagree, seqforge asks you.

docs.title: How an entry is aligned
docs.text:
Each entry names the pipeline that aligns it:

Pipeline Used for What it writes per sample STARsolo, the single-cell mode of the STAR aligner 10x RNA, BD Rhapsody, SPLiT-seq A count matrix (.h5ad) STAR with gene counts Bulk RNA-seq Gene counts STAR with UMI counting Smart-seq3 One count matrix for the whole plate chromap, a fast aligner for chromatin data Multiome ATAC A fragments file (fragments.tsv.gz)

docs.title: Add a technology
docs.text:
Every entry is executable. It declares its chemistry precisely enough that seqforge can write synthetic reads from it, read them back, and check that it recovers what it declared. To teach seqforge a new chemistry, follow Add a technology.

For drawings of each library's structure, the Teichmann Lab's scg_lib_structs is a good reference. Each assay page links to its entry there where one exists.

docs.title: 10x Chromium Single Cell 3' Gene Expression v2
docs.text: Droplet single-cell RNA-seq with 10x Genomics' second-generation 3' kit, the one before v3. Each droplet holds one gel bead. The bead tags every transcript of its cell with the same cell barcode, and each mRNA molecule with its own UMI (unique molecular identifier, a random tag). Together they let you count molecules per gene per cell.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
Read Length What it holds R1 26 bp a 16 bp cell barcode, then a 10 bp UMI R2 any length the cDNA (the transcript itself), read in the same direction as the mRNA

The cell barcodes come from 10x's 737K-august-2016 list, about 737,000 barcodes.

docs.title: How seqforge tells v2 from v3
docs.text:
v2's R1 is 16 + 10 = 26 bp. v3's is 16 + 12 = 28 bp. When R1 is the canonical length, that 2 bp difference settles it before any barcode list is checked.

Some runs sequence R1 long, to 100 bp or more. Then both kits accept the read, and the barcode list decides: v2 uses 737K-august-2016 and v3 uses 3M-february-2018.

If a paper or record says "v2" while the reads say v3, seqforge does not quietly pick one. It reports the disagreement and asks you. The bytes decide what the data is.

docs.title: The one neighbour the reads cannot settle
docs.text:
10x 5' v1 and v2 match this kit in every byte. They have the same 26 bp R1 (16 bp barcode and 10 bp UMI), the same cDNA R2, and the same 737K-august-2016 barcode list. So neither the read layout nor the list can tell them apart.

The two are aligned differently in one setting: the strand. 5' kits read the transcript from the other end. No check on the reads can see that.

So this is the only pair in the knowledge base that the reads cannot settle. seqforge turns to the paper or the archive record, which name "5'" or "3'" reliably even when they are vague about the version. A trial alignment can also settle it. If neither does, seqforge asks you.

The risk is real. Before the 5' entry existed, a 5' library was read as this kit and aligned on the wrong strand. Its gene expression correlated with the right answer at only 0.5 to 0.6 (more than 0.98 on the right strand), and the run still exited with no error.

v3 has no such twin: each kit that shares its 28 bp layout has its own barcode list.

docs.title: What goes wrong
docs.text:
• The barcode read can go missing on SRA. fasterq-dump without --include-technical drops R1. seqforge then stops rather than guessing which file is which. Fetch the data again with --include-technical, or download the submitter's original files.
  • SRA rewrites read names, so seqforge never uses them to group files into samples.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The read structure is checked against scg_lib_structs: 10x Chromium 3' (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY), which shows the v2 to v4 kits side by side. The exact definition seqforge runs is this entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: 10x Chromium Single Cell 3' Gene Expression v3 (and v3.1)
docs.text:
Droplet single-cell RNA-seq with 10x Genomics' third-generation 3' kit. Each droplet holds one gel bead. The bead tags every transcript of its cell with the same cell barcode, and each mRNA molecule with its own UMI (unique molecular identifier, a random tag that lets you count molecules rather than reads).

This page covers both v3 and v3.1. To a sequencer they are the same library, and seqforge processes them the same way. See v3 vs v3.1 below.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
Read Length What it holds R1 28 bp a 16 bp cell barcode, then a 12 bp UMI R2 any length the cDNA (the transcript itself), read in the same direction as the mRNA

The cell barcodes come from 10x's 3M-february-2018 list, about 6.8 million barcodes. Index reads (I1, I2) may be present or not. seqforge does not need them.

Names you'll see in papers and records: "10x 3' v3", "Chromium 3' v3", "SC3Pv3", "single cell 3-prime v3", "Next GEM 3' v3.1". A paper often writes "10x 3' v3" for a v3.1 run, or names the kit without a version. That changes nothing, as the next section explains.

docs.title: v3 vs v3.1
docs.text: To seqforge the two are identical: the same read layout, the same barcode list, the same alignment settings. No check on the reads can tell them apart, and none needs to. So seqforge records both names and asks you nothing. v3.1 has its own knowledge-base entry only so that the test suite checks on every build that the two really are identical.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it from other kits
docs.text:
• 3' v2 has a 10 bp UMI, so its R1 is 26 bp, not 28 bp. When R1 is the canonical length, that 2 bp difference settles it. When R1 was sequenced long (100 bp or more), both kits accept it, and the barcode list decides: v2 uses a different list.
  • Multiome gene expression, GEM-X 3' v4 and GEM-X 5' v3 all have the same 28 bp layout, with a 16 bp barcode and a 12 bp UMI. Each uses its own barcode list, so seqforge checks which list the barcodes hit. The read layout narrows the choice to these four, and the list picks one. 5' v3 also reads the cDNA in the other direction, but the reads cannot show that. Its list is what settles it.
  • The pair the reads cannot settle is one generation back: 3' v2 against 5' v1 and v2. It does not involve v3. See the 3' v2 page.

docs.title: What goes wrong
docs.text:
• The barcode read can go missing on SRA. fasterq-dump without --include-technical drops the 28 bp R1. seqforge then stops rather than inventing a barcode read from a file name. Fetch the data again with --include-technical, or download the submitter's original files.
  • A pre-trimmed upload no longer has R1 at one fixed length, which moves the barcode. seqforge refuses rather than reading the barcode from the wrong place.
  • SRA rewrites read names, so seqforge never uses them to group files into samples.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The read structure is checked against scg_lib_structs: 10x Chromium 3' (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY). The exact definition seqforge runs is each entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: BD Rhapsody WTA (Whole Transcriptome Analysis)
docs.text:
Single-cell 3' RNA-seq from BD Biosciences, with no droplets. Cells settle into the wells of a microwell cartridge, one per well, together with a capture bead. The bead tags each cell's transcripts with a cell label built from three barcode blocks, and each molecule with a UMI (unique molecular identifier, a random tag).

BD has sold two bead generations. seqforge recognizes and compiles both from the reads, so you never have to say which bead a dataset used. The original bead, with every block at a fixed place, comes first below. The 2022 Enhanced bead follows.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
• R2 is the cDNA (the transcript), read in the same direction as the mRNA.
  • R1 is the bead read: three 9 bp cell-label blocks separated by two fixed linker sequences, then an 8 bp UMI.
Part of R1 Length Bases cell label 1 9 bp 1 to 9 linker 1 (ACTGGCCTGCGA) 12 bp 10 to 21 cell label 2 9 bp 22 to 30 linker 2 (GGTAGCGGTGACA) 13 bp 31 to 43 cell label 3 9 bp 44 to 52 UMI 8 bp 53 to 60

Each cell-label block comes from its own list of 97 9-mers, so there are 97³, about 913,000, possible cell labels. R1 is often sequenced past base 60 into the poly(T) stretch and the cDNA. seqforge ignores those extra bases.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it apart
docs.text: The two fixed linkers at known places are the signature. No other supported kit has them. Each cell-label block also matches its own barcode list. That confirms the call, and it separates BD Rhapsody from plain paired-end bulk RNA-seq, which has no barcode list to match.

docs.title: Strand
docs.text: The bead's capture oligo ends in poly(dT), which binds the mRNA's poly(A) tail. So R2 reads the cDNA in the same direction as the transcript, as in any 3' poly(dT) library such as 10x 3'. A wrong strand would leave most reads uncounted while the aligner still exits with no error, so seqforge takes the strand from the bead chemistry rather than guessing.

docs.title: Enhanced beads (2022)
docs.text:
In 2022 BD introduced Enhanced Cell Capture Beads, the current chemistry. The cell labels work the same way, three 9 bp blocks read off the bead, but two things change:

  • A short diversity insert of 0 to 3 bases (nothing, A, GT or TCA) comes at the very start of R1. It staggers the reads so the sequencer needs less PhiX control DNA.
  • The two linkers shrink to GTGA and GACA, 4 bp each, from the original bead's 12 bp and 13 bp.

So an Enhanced R1 reads:

[0-3 bp insert] [cell label 1, 9 bp] GTGA [cell label 2, 9 bp] GACA [cell label 3, 9 bp] [UMI, 8 bp]

There are two versions, which differ only in their cell-label lists. BD calls them 96-plex and 384-plex. The 96-plex bead uses the same lists as the original bead (97 barcodes each). The 384-plex bead uses three lists of 384 barcodes, which allow more cell labels. The read layout is the same.

docs.title: How seqforge handles the Enhanced bead
docs.text:
You do not name the bead generation, and you do not trim the diversity insert.

  • Recognition. The insert moves every barcode by a different amount from one read to the next, so no position is fixed. seqforge finds the GTGA...GACA frame in each read, allowing for the 0 to 3 base stagger and for sequencing errors, and reads the cell labels and the UMI relative to it. That frame is what separates the Enhanced bead from the original one, whose longer linkers sit at fixed places.
  • 96-plex or 384-plex. The two have the same read layout, so seqforge picks the one whose lists the barcodes hit. It tells 10x v2 from v3 the same way when the reads are long. Both sets of lists ship with seqforge.
  • Alignment. STARsolo, the single-cell mode of the STAR aligner, can find the linker frame by itself. seqforge computes the settings from the read layout, the ones STAR's author endorsed in STAR issue 1607:
STAR --soloType CB_UMI_Complex \
     --soloAdapterSequence NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA \
     --soloCBposition 2_0_2_8 2_13_2_21 3_1_3_9 \
     --soloUMIposition 3_10_3_17 \
     --soloCBwhitelist BD_CLS1.txt BD_CLS2.txt BD_CLS3.txt

The adapter NNNNNNNNNGTGANNNNNNNNNGACA is cell label 1 (9 bases), GTGA, cell label 2 (9 bases) and GACA. STARsolo finds it in each read and reads the barcodes relative to it, so the insert at the front needs no special step. For a reference workflow that covers every bead generation, see rhapsodist.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The read structure, linker sequences and barcode lists are taken from scg_lib_structs: BD Rhapsody (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY), and checked against the seqspec bd_rhapsody_v1 example and the settings the STAR author endorsed. The exact definition seqforge runs is in spec.yaml, in this folder and in the Enhanced entries' folders.

docs.title: Bulk Illumina RNA-seq
docs.text: Standard bulk RNA-seq on an Illumina sequencer: cDNA reads with no cell barcode and no UMI. Every base is transcript sequence, and there are no cells to separate. seqforge aligns these reads with plain STAR and counts reads per gene, instead of using STARsolo, STAR's single-cell mode.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
• R1 and R2 are the two ends of the same cDNA fragment, a mate pair. Both are transcript sequence, usually 75 to 150 bp. seqforge accepts 40 to 300 bp.
  • There is no barcode, no UMI and no barcode list.

Paired-end and single-end are one entry. They are the same chemistry, sequenced two ways. The entry declares the paired layout and names R1 alone as its single-end form, and the bytes choose between them. A deposit with one file per run is read as single-end, not refused. The reads are described once, so the two forms cannot drift apart.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it from single-cell data
docs.text:
The absence of a barcode read identifies bulk. seqforge looks for a short technical read whose first bases repeat across many reads, which is what a cell barcode looks like. In bulk data it finds none: only two long cDNA mates whose reads are almost all different from the first base. A 10x barcode read is 26 or 28 bp and repeats the same 16 bp barcodes, so it is never mistaken for bulk cDNA.

Because this entry demands so little, it also accepts almost any pair of reads. That is on purpose: it is the fallback for paired-end data. It also means some single-cell kits look like bulk on the first, cheap checks. seqforge then settles each case on firmer evidence:

Kit that can look like bulk What settles it BD Rhapsody (both beads), SPLiT-seq Their barcode lists. Bulk has no list to match 10x Multiome, chromatin (ATAC) arm Its barcode read matches the Multiome ATAC list Smart-seq3 The paper or archive record. Neither kit has a barcode list, so if the record does not say, seqforge asks you

So seqforge never quietly treats a single-cell library as bulk.

docs.title: Coverage note
docs.text: This entry is for poly(A)-selected libraries. seqforge does not model a strand protocol for bulk data yet.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The exact definition seqforge runs is this entry's spec.yaml. scg_lib_structs documents single-cell library structures, and plain bulk RNA-seq is not one of them, so there is no page to link.

docs.title: SPLiT-seq (split-pool combinatorial barcoding)
docs.text:
Single-cell RNA-seq that needs no special instrument. Instead of one droplet per cell, cells are split into the wells of a plate, labelled, pooled, and split again, for three rounds. After three rounds, each cell carries its own combination of three barcodes.

This entry covers the original published SPLiT-seq (Rosenberg et al., Science 2018). Parse Biosciences' Evercode is a commercial descendant with different linkers and barcode positions. It is a different chemistry, and seqforge does not cover it.

docs.title: How it's read
docs.text:
• Read 1 is the cDNA (the transcript), read in the same direction as the mRNA.
  • Read 2 is the barcode read, exactly 94 bp: a 10 bp UMI (unique molecular identifier, a random tag on each molecule), then three 8 bp round barcodes separated by two fixed 30 bp linkers.
[10 bp UMI] [8 bp round 3] [30 bp linker 1] [8 bp round 2] [30 bp linker 2] [8 bp round 1]

A cell's identity is the combination of its round 1, round 2 and round 3 barcodes. Each round draws from a list of 96 barcodes, and all three lists ship with seqforge.

The cDNA read can start with the method's template-switch oligo, a 30-base sequence the library preparation adds. The compiled pipeline clips SPLiT-seq's own version of it, which differs from 10x's at two of thirty bases.

docs.title: How seqforge tells it apart
docs.text:
As for BD Rhapsody, the two fixed linker sequences at known places are the signature, and each round barcode matches its own list. The exact positions matter. The original 2018 chemistry puts the round 1 barcode at bases 87 to 94 of Read 2, counting from 1, while Parse's chemistry puts it eight bases earlier. A position copied from the wrong source silently misses. seqforge takes the original layout from the paper's own oligo table, and real data from the paper (GEO series GSE110823) confirms it.

The barcode lists also separate SPLiT-seq from plain paired-end bulk RNA-seq, which has no list to match.

docs.title: One open question: the strand
docs.text: The strand has not yet been confirmed by aligning real data. seqforge derives it from the paper's oligos, and the authors' own pipeline agrees. No source claims the opposite. But most pipelines never chose a strand; they kept the aligner's default. So their agreement is weaker evidence than it looks. The decisive check is to align the paper's own data both ways: the right strand should assign far more reads to genes.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The read structure and linker sequences are taken from scg_lib_structs: SPLiT-seq (Teichmann Lab, CC-BY), and rebuilt on their own from the paper's oligo tables (Rosenberg et al., Science 2018). The exact definition seqforge runs is this entry's spec.yaml.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Every seqforge command, one line each, grouped by what you want to do. For a command's options, run it with --help, for example seqforge study run --help. The help is always current.

The Needs column names what a command uses beyond your own files:

  • Gateway: the lab's model gateway, at $LABLLM_GATEWAY. The command spends money and takes a --ceiling-usd.
  • Stores: liulab-data's record store ($LABDATA_STORE), paper store ($LABDATA_PAPERS) and ontology store ($LABDATA_ONTOLOGIES).
  • Network: the public archives (NCBI, the US archive, and ENA, the European one) or a web address.
  • Genome: liulab-genome, for the genome and its gene annotation.
  • Cluster: a step the compiled pipeline runs on the cluster, next to the aligner. You do not run it by hand.

A blank cell means the command needs none of these.

docs.title: Read studies
docs.text:
Command What it does Needs seqforge study run Bound and then read each study of a folder, under one spending limit Gateway, Stores seqforge pass start Run one job, study-bounds or study-reading, over its studies Gateway, Stores seqforge pass status Say where a job stands: the count of each ending, the cost, and each study not done seqforge study write-bounds Write each study's bounds file from the bounding job's answers seqforge study write-reading Write each study's reading file from the reading job's answers liulab-data installed seqforge study check-bounds Check one bounds file against its format seqforge study check-reading Check one reading file against its format liulab-data installed seqforge study relations Print the relations between the samples of one reading: replicates, contrasts, series and controls liulab-data installed seqforge standard-set list List the 50 studies of the standard set, from each study's files

The few options you need for study run are --studies (the folder), --ceiling-usd (the most it may spend, required) and --keys (a file of Series ids, one per line). Read your own studies walks through them.

docs.title: Compile a dataset
docs.text:
Command What it does Needs seqforge run FASTQ files and notes in, manifest and pipeline out, in one command. seqforge compile is the same command Gateway unless --no-llm; Network or Stores with --accession; Genome seqforge probe Read the start of each FASTQ file and report what the reads look like seqforge resolve score Decide which technology the reads are, from their bytes and the knowledge base seqforge io records Fetch what the archive says about an accession: project, samples, experiments and runs Network, or the record store seqforge io resolve Expand an accession into its runs, and flag a read the archive dropped Network seqforge records new Draft a record set: which FASTQ files in a folder compile together seqforge records validate Check a record set and say what it declares seqforge harvest normalize Turn each document, such as a PDF or a spreadsheet, into the text that quotes are checked against seqforge harvest extract Ask a model to read claims out of a document, each with a quote Gateway seqforge harvest verify Find each quote in the document again and check that it backs its value seqforge manifest fill Write the dataset manifest: what the data is Network or the record store with --accession seqforge manifest validate Check a manifest seqforge manifest hash Print a manifest's content hash, and whether it matches the one recorded seqforge processing new Write a recipe: what to do with the data, such as the genome to align to seqforge processing validate Check a recipe seqforge processing hash Print a recipe's content hash, and whether it matches the one recorded seqforge compose Compile a manifest and a recipe into a Snakefile, its config and its table of input files Genome seqforge project metadata Rewrite the sample table and the project file from each assay's manifest

Compile step by step runs these in order on a real dataset.

docs.title: Check the knowledge base
docs.text:
The knowledge base is the list of sequencing technologies seqforge knows. Each entry describes its reads and tests itself.

Command What it does Needs seqforge kb list List every technology seqforge kb show Print one technology's entry as JSON seqforge kb lint Check every entry against its schema seqforge kb roundtrip Make fake reads for one technology and check that seqforge recognizes them seqforge kb e2e Run fake reads through the aligner and check the count table against what went in Genome, and the STAR aligner seqforge kb e2e-introns The same, with reads from introns, to check that the two ways of counting differ as they should Genome, and the STAR aligner seqforge kb e2e-cost Measure the aligner's peak memory against the number of reads Genome, and the STAR aligner seqforge kb e2e-fit Fit one line across cost runs measured separately

Add a technology shows how an entry is written and tested.

docs.title: Look at results
docs.text:
Command What it does Needs seqforge report Write one HTML page and its JSON data for a compile, a study, or both liulab-data installed for a study seqforge eval report Write an HTML page from an eval run result

seqforge report --study <folder>/<ID> alone makes a study's report in its folder. Without --study, it reports on the compile in the current folder, or in the folder --workspace names.

docs.title: Network and files
docs.text: Command What it does Needs seqforge io peek Read the start of a remote compressed FASTQ file without downloading it Network seqforge io probe-remote Report what a remote FASTQ file's reads look like, without downloading it Network seqforge io probe-sra Report what an SRA run's reads look like, without downloading it Network seqforge preflight Pack the start of each FASTQ file and the notes into one small file that compiles the same way Network with --accession seqforge strip-fingerprint Repack that file without the paper and its figures, so it can be shared seqforge io publish-package Publish that file to the public benchmark collection Network seqforge io onlist list List the barcode lists seqforge ships seqforge io onlist show Show one barcode list's entry as JSON seqforge io onlist write Write a barcode list as the text the aligner reads Cluster seqforge io onlist pack Pack a barcode list into the shipped form. For maintainers

docs.text:
The Snakefile calls these after alignment. Each needs the cluster.

Command What it does seqforge io h5ad Package the aligner's count tables as an .h5ad file, the format single-cell tools read seqforge io h5ad-labels Add the sample table's labels to one sample's .h5ad file seqforge io qc-bundle Bundle one sample's statistics and logs into one file seqforge io fragments Sort, compress and index the fragments file of an ATAC library (open chromatin) seqforge io fragments-qc Summarize a fragments file seqforge io cram Store the aligned reads as a CRAM file, a smaller form of a BAM file, the standard file of aligned reads seqforge io umi-extract Move a plate assay's UMI, the molecule tag, out of the first read seqforge io umi-count Count every cell of a plate into one .h5ad file seqforge io split-chimera Split reads aligned to two genomes at once into one file per genome

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Every command reports its result through its exit code.

Code Meaning 0 It worked 1 Something broke, such as a download or a tool that failed 2 It could not start: a wrong option, a file it cannot read, or a missing gateway or store. Nothing was spent 3 Blocked or stopped: the data cannot go on as it is, a file failed its check, or a pass reached its spending limit 4 A person must decide: two sources disagree, or a quote did not check out

A command's own --help says which of these it can return.

docs.title: Add a technology to the knowledge base
docs.text:
seqforge knows a sequencing technology only if its knowledge base has an entry for it. This page walks through adding one: you describe the reads in a spec.yaml file, then prove the description with seqforge's self-test. It is for a contributor who knows the assay's read structure and wants seqforge to recognize and compile it.

The rule that makes an entry trustworthy: every entry is executable and tests itself. From your description seqforge writes synthetic reads, reads them back with its normal code, and checks that it recovers what you declared. You need no real data and no download for that first test.

docs.title: What an entry is
docs.text:
Each technology has one folder under src/seqforge/kb/specs/:

src/seqforge/kb/specs/<technology-id>/
    spec.yaml     for the machine: the read layout, the barcode positions, how to detect it, how to align it
    README.md     for a person: how the assay works, what it is confused with, what goes wrong

The README becomes the assay's page on this site, so write it for a biologist. Keep the reasoning behind each value (strand derivations, why two entries are told apart) as comments in spec.yaml. No code reads the README. spec.yaml is what seqforge runs.

docs.title: Start from the nearest entry
docs.text:
There is no command that writes a blank entry. Copy the folder of the closest existing technology and edit it:

Your assay's cell barcode Copy One block at a fixed place in one read 10x-3p-gex-v3 Several blocks separated by fixed linker sequences splitseq or bd-rhapsody-wta Behind a variable-length insert, found by its linkers bd-rhapsody-wta-enhanced-v1

seqforge kb list lists every entry. seqforge kb show <technology-id> prints one entry as seqforge loaded and checked it.

docs.title: Fill in spec.yaml
docs.text:
A spec.yaml has these parts:

Part What it says identity The id, version and name; aliases, the names papers use for it; assay_ontology, its Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO) term; modality, such as rna reads Each read, its length range, and its elements in order: barcode, umi, cdna, linker, and others, each with its position onlists The barcode lists the barcodes come from, by their registered name signature How to detect it: requires (checks that must pass), supports (evidence that adds to its score), excludes (checks that rule it out) backend Which pipeline aligns it, and the aligner settings the read layout fixes parent The family it belongs to, if any, such as 10x-3p-gex confusable_with Every entry whose reads look like yours, and what tells the two apart

Look up every value. Write none from memory.

  • The ontology term. Check it in the lab's ontology store (labdata ontology search efo <text>). A remembered term id is usually plausible and wrong.
  • The read structure, linkers and positions. Take them from the primary paper's oligo tables or from scg_lib_structs, and name the kit version. SPLiT-seq's first-round barcode sits at bases 87 to 94 of the barcode read, counting from 1, in the original method, and eight bases earlier in its commercial descendant. A remembered position can be either.
  • The strand. Derive it from the oligo orientation and record the derivation in a comment. A wrong strand leaves most reads uncounted while the aligner exits with no error.
  • The aligner's barcode positions. Leave them out. seqforge computes them from the element positions you declared when it writes the pipeline.

Each element has a fixed start and end, or an anchor to a neighbouring element. A barcode behind a variable-length insert needs an anchor, as in the BD Rhapsody Enhanced entries.

docs.title: Say how to read the bytes, never what to count
docs.text: backend.params holds only what the bytes decide: where the barcode starts, how long it is, which strand. What to count (the aligner's count features) belongs in the recipe, because the same chemistry can be used for cells or for nuclei. seqforge refuses a spec that puts a counting setting in backend.params. When one did, it cost a measured 40.7% of a single-nucleus library.

docs.title: Ship the barcode lists
docs.text:
An entry whose barcodes are told apart by a barcode list must ship that list. Pack each list into seqforge's own format:

seqforge io onlist pack <list.txt.gz> --name <list-name> \
  --uri <where-it-came-from> --orientation forward

This writes the packed list and updates the index in src/seqforge/io/onlists/. Commit both files. Take the sequences from an authoritative source. Without the list, the self-test still passes, but real reads score as bulk RNA-seq and compile to the wrong pipeline at exit 0.

docs.title: Declare what your entry is confused with
docs.text:
Some technologies cannot be told apart from their reads alone. 10x 3' v3 and v3.1 share the same read layout and the same barcode list. That is a fact about the chemistry, so write it down:

confusable_with:
  - id: some-other-tech
    relationship: processing_equivalent   # or processing_divergent
    distinguishable_by: [onlist]          # what can tell them apart
    note: >
      Why they collide, in a sentence someone can check.
  • processing_equivalent: the two are aligned with identical settings, so the difference changes nothing. seqforge records both names and asks nothing.
  • processing_divergent: the two need different pipelines. Something must tell them apart: usually a barcode list (onlist), otherwise the metadata (metadata) or a trial alignment (alignment). If nothing in the data settles it, seqforge stops and asks a person (exit 4).

You cannot skip this. The test suite makes reads from each entry and asks every other entry whether it would claim them on the cheap checks alone. An overlap you did not declare fails the suite. Declare each one on both entries. A plain paired-end entry, bulk-rnaseq, accepts almost any pair of reads, so a new barcoded entry usually needs a processing_divergent edge to it, told apart by onlist.

docs.title: Run the self-test
docs.text:
These run on your machine and need nothing else.

pixi run -- seqforge kb lint                       # every spec against the schema
pixi run -- seqforge kb roundtrip <technology-id>  # declared == recovered
pixi run -- seqforge kb show <technology-id>       # read it back as seqforge loaded it
  • kb lint checks every entry against the schema. It fails at the line where a typo or an unknown word sits, and on any counting setting in backend.params. It exits 3 if any entry is invalid.
  • kb roundtrip writes synthetic reads from your reads section, runs them through the same code that reads real files, and compares what comes back with what you declared. It exits 3 on any difference. A linker sequence one base longer than its window shifts every later element, and this is where that shows.

Then run the tests that compare entries in pairs:

pixi run -e test pytest tests/test_kb.py -k "confusable or biconditional"

They report each pair of entries whose reads overlap with no declared relationship. They pick up a new entry because its folder exists, so there is nothing to register.

docs.title: Before you open a pull request
docs.text:
1. Check the entry against real reads from one public dataset. A wrong strand or a wrong barcode list passes every simulated test, because a simulation tests your description against itself.
  2. Write the README for a person: what the assay is, how it is read, how seqforge tells it from its neighbours, what goes wrong, and a link to its scg_lib_structs page if it has one.

  3. Run the repository's gate once:

    pixi run check
